words.definition: The stage of development when the body matures toward adulthood and becomes capable of reproduction.
The shedding of the uterine lining, which leaves the body through the vagina as bleeding.
A change in which tissue in the penis or clitoris becomes firmer as it fills with blood.
The release of an egg from an ovary.
A muscular organ where a pregnancy can develop.
Two organs that contain eggs and make hormones such as estrogen and progesterone.
Two organs that make sperm and hormones such as testosterone.
Reproductive cells that can fertilize an egg.
The growth of breast tissue, often beginning during puberty.
Hair that grows on parts of the body such as the arms, legs, underarms, or groin.
A period when the body gets taller or larger more quickly than usual.
A shift in how high or low someone sounds, often as the voice box grows during puberty.
A skin condition that causes pimples, blackheads, or other bumps when pores become clogged.
Liquid released through the skin that helps cool the body.
The smell that can develop when skin bacteria break down sweat and other secretions.
Chemical messengers that help control processes such as growth, mood, and reproduction.
A hormone that helps regulate sexual development, muscle, and bone growth.
A group of hormones involved in sexual development, menstrual cycles, and bone health.
A small gland at the base of the brain that releases hormones controlling growth and other glands.
The external genital area that includes the labia, clitoris, and vaginal opening.
An external genital organ through which urine and semen can leave the body.
The pouch of skin that contains and helps regulate the temperature of the testes.
The muscular canal connecting the outside of the body to the cervix.
Two narrow passages through which an egg can travel from an ovary toward the uterus.

name: Sex education
description: Medium–challenge; opt-in sexual and reproductive health vocabulary.

words.definition: A thin barrier used during sex to reduce the chance of pregnancy or sexually transmitted infections.
Methods or devices used to prevent pregnancy.
A liquid or gel used to reduce friction between surfaces, including skin.
A test that checks urine or blood for a hormone produced during pregnancy.
A small device placed inside the uterus by a health professional to prevent pregnancy.
A vaccine that protects against types of human papillomavirus that can cause cancers or genital warts.
Testing for sexually transmitted infections, including when a person has no symptoms.
The ability to contribute to or achieve a pregnancy.
Health care and checkups during pregnancy before the baby is born.
The point when menstrual periods have stopped for 12 months in a row without another cause.
A medicine taken by mouth on a schedule to help prevent pregnancy.
A small rod placed under the skin that releases a hormone to prevent pregnancy.
An adhesive worn on the skin that releases hormones to prevent pregnancy.
A method used after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure to reduce the chance of pregnancy.
A thin sheet used as a barrier during oral sex to help reduce infection risk.
An absorbent strip worn inside underwear to catch menstrual fluid.
A small absorbent product inserted into the vagina to absorb menstrual fluid.
A flexible container worn inside the vagina that collects menstrual fluid.
Underwear designed with layers that absorb menstrual fluid.
A health service that offers care such as infection testing, contraception, or advice.
Checking for changes or infections linked to cancer of the cervix.
The condition that begins when a fertilized egg has begun to develop and implants, usually in the lining of the uterus.
A virus that attacks the immune system and can lead to AIDS without treatment.
Talking with a trained professional about sexual well-being, concerns, or care options.

name: Consent
description: Medium–challenge; opt-in consent and personal-boundary concepts.

words.definition: A freely given agreement to a specific activity that a person can withdraw at any time.
Limits people set about what they are comfortable with or willing to take part in.
The ability to control who can access your personal information, space, or experiences.
An act of saying or showing that you do not agree or do not want to take part.
Treating someone as a person whose choices, feelings, and limits matter.
Sharing and receiving information, thoughts, or feelings so others can understand you.
The area around your body where you feel comfortable keeping some distance from others.
A person's right to decide what happens to their own body.
Using pressure, threats, or force to get someone to do something they would not freely choose.
Briefly asking how someone feels or whether they are still comfortable continuing.
Deciding differently after making an earlier choice or agreement.
Paying close attention to what someone says and checking that you understood them.
Keeping information private when it has been shared in confidence.
Stating what you need, think, or want clearly while respecting others.
Physical contact that the person receiving it does not want or agree to.
A state in which alcohol or other drugs affect judgment, awareness, or movement.
A situation where one person has more authority or influence than another.
An absence of speech or response, which by itself does not show agreement.
A pause or reluctance that can signal uncertainty or discomfort.
Asking for or giving more information to make something easier to understand.
Sending, posting, or showing a photo or another picture to someone else.
Taking safe action when you witness a situation in which someone may be harmed.
Taking responsibility for your actions and addressing their effects on others.
Trying to control someone's choices unfairly or dishonestly for your own benefit.
